So let me know if you have any questions. I had a shower thought that turned into a super basic, bare bones model. Let me know what you think:

  1. Find tenants who would want to purchase a year's worth of rent at a discounted price.

  2. Upon purchasing discounted rent, my business would be liable to pay each of their rents in full every month.

  3. Since there is time before all the rent needs to be paid, the business invests the money to make it grow to an amount higher than that is necessary to pay all the rent.

  4. Rinse and Repeat (no growth in the amount of tenants to keep the same amount coming in and the profit after investments will keep compounding every year)

I am already seeing holes, but let me know what you think. maybe we can iron out the kinks together. like i said, its just a silly shower thought that i was molding in my head all day.

Edit: sorry fellas, I got confused. My title should be [IDEA] as this was just a small lightbulb moment one day. I'm not looking to move forward unless someone wants to work it through and maybe has any sort of idea to iron out the kinks

It's a very interesting concept. You'd have to very carefully choose your investments though, since a small mistake/loss could potentially result in a tenant not getting their rent paid, or you could be forced to take a loan yourself - Having the same interest rate on both your investment and load won't get you anywhere.

I'm not sure how rental agreements work, but I think it's usually between just the tenant and the estate agent - I'm not sure how it stands legally to have a business pay it on your behalf.

Sounds like a possibly decent idea, but there's a pretty high initial risk and a lot of issues to work out like you said.

From what I'm reading, it'd be a scenario like this, and farmer-, please feel free to correct me.

Let's pretend that my monthly rent will be $1,000 for the year. I sign up with this company, and agree to pay them $1,000 each month.
The company has $11,000, and is planning on investing in such a way to receive enough money to cover the entire rent

The main issue i see with it, since this is such a short timeframe, you'd essentially have to get lucky to ensure you don't lose money on the deal. 11k --> 12k is almost a 10% return over the course of a year, which, while definitely possible, is an outperformance of standard market rates (long term), and is not something that can be reliably banked on.

And if you have one year where a recession hits, you're suddenly liable for thousands upon thousands of rent payments (especially if you get more than one client).

All in all, I think it would be rough to ensure that you can grow your funds to cover it that well.

You'd also have to deal with what happens if a tenant splits in the middle of the night. It basically seems like you're taking the risk of a landlord, without actually owning the property, for minimal gain (essentially interest).

your criticism is correct, but the person is not paying 1,000 each month. they are paying a year's worth of rent lump-sum at the beginning of the year. say the entire year's worth of rent for one person magically ended up being 10,000. if they bought discounted rent at a 10% discount, the person would pay 9,000 on January 1st, 20XX and for the rest of the year would not have to make a single rent payment. The person would be covered for the entire year while the business would have to pay his/her rent monthly. The lump sum in the beginning is what is giving me the idea that maybe one could throw all the money into investments sooner and let it grow throughout the year while it slowly gets paid away into monthly rent installments to the landlord.

Ahh, I follow.

This would then apply to a very small group of clients, since most people (especially renters) don't have enough saved to pay their entire year's worth of rent in one go.

You'd still be in a sticky situation if the market goes south, since one year is such a short you're horizon, you're not really giving the capital room to grow.

The s&p averages a 7%(ish) per year, over any 30 year span. But that gives it enough time to get out of recessions.

If you started this on early 2008, you'd be on the hook for a lot of rent payments that you'd have to find the capital to cover, considering your investments might have lost 20 to 30 percent

The only thing I can think of is figuring out what your return would be vs. the discount you would offer. I mean, how much of a discount would be important. The liability would be how you'd invest the money to turn a profit. There is also the matter of someone having to break a lease due to relocation for job purposes, though that would be rare.

Would your company be liable for deposits lost due to property damage? Would clients pay the entire year up front? In many rental situations, they may not have those kinds of funds. And, if they don't front the discounted rate for the year, how would you invest the monthly payments? It seems like you may have to take a riskier approach to investing to get a return to offset the discount offered, since many leases are short-term.

It seems like you'd have to have some kind of fee schedule to reduce the risk on your end, which unless the discount is high enough, would have the tenant break-even. For some reason, I'm likening this idea to micro-financing, only in reverse. . . if that makes sense.
